title: The Ram, the Goat, and the Little Horn
summary: In a vision at Susa, Daniel sees a two-horned ram overrun by a swift goat with one great horn, which breaks and is replaced by four horns. From one of them a little horn grows, attacks the heavenly host, stops the daily sacrifice, and throws down the sanctuary. The angel Gabriel explains that the ram is Media and Persia, the goat is Greece, and the little horn is a fierce king who will be broken, but not by human hands.
story: With this chapter the book returns to Hebrew and to a narrower focus. Chapter 7 surveyed four kingdoms and the end of history; chapter 8 zooms in on the second and third, Persia and Greece, and on one king who will arise from the Greek world to attack God's people and their worship. Here, unusually, the kingdoms are named (verses 20 and 21), which anchors the symbolism. The little horn of this chapter becomes the central threat of the rest of the book: chapter 11 will trace the same king's career in detail. The chapter's question, "How long" (verse 13), is the cry of the persecuted, and the answer sets a limit to the desolation.
historical:
The vision is dated to Belshazzar's third year, probably in the early 540s BC, while Babylon still stood. Susa, the capital of the old kingdom of Elam east of Babylon, would become one of the royal capitals of the Persian Empire; the Ulai was a canal or river beside it. Daniel is there in the vision, not necessarily in body.

The symbols match known history closely, and interpreters of every school agree on most of them. The ram's two horns are Media and Persia, the longer and later one Persia, which under Cyrus came to dominate the Medes and pushed west, north, and south. The goat is Greece, and its great horn is Alexander the Great, who crossed from Europe in 334 BC and defeated the Persian Empire with astonishing speed, as if not touching the ground. He died in Babylon in 323 BC at the height of his power, and his empire was divided among his generals into four main kingdoms, centered on Macedonia, Thrace and Asia Minor, Syria and Mesopotamia (the Seleucids), and Egypt (the Ptolemies). The little horn that grows toward the south, the east, and the Beautiful Land (Judea) is widely identified as Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175 to 164 BC), the Seleucid king who campaigned in Egypt and the east, stopped the temple sacrifices in 167 BC, and set up pagan worship in the sanctuary until Judas Maccabeus rededicated it in December 164 BC. Some interpreters also see him as a pattern of a final opponent of God.
cultural:
Rams and goats were natural symbols of leaders, since they lead flocks, and horns stood for power throughout the Old Testament. Some scholars note that in ancient astrology the ram and the goat were linked with the regions of Persia and Syria, though whether the vision draws on that association is uncertain.

The daily sacrifice (verse 11) was the burnt offering presented each morning and evening at the temple (Exodus 29:38-42), the heartbeat of Israel's worship. To stop it was to silence the covenant relationship at its center. The host of heaven and the stars (verse 10) can refer to angels or to stars, and here probably to God's people, whose earthly struggle is mirrored in heaven. Antiochus took the title Epiphanes, meaning god made manifest, and the Greek historian Polybius reports that some mocked him as Epimanes, the madman. The chapter's language of a king who magnifies himself even to the Prince of the host captures a ruler who made himself the equal of God.
literary: The chapter follows the pattern of chapter 7: a dated vision, the vision itself (verses 3 to 14), and an interpretation by a heavenly figure (verses 15 to 26), ending with Daniel's distress. Its imagery is less fantastic than chapter 7's, with real animals rather than hybrids, and its interpretation is more explicit. The verb to magnify or become great recurs through the vision (verses 4, 8, 9, 10, 11, 25), tracing the rise of each power until the last one exalts itself against God. This is the first time in the Bible an angel is named: Gabriel, whose name means something like God is my strength or mighty man of God. He addresses Daniel as "Son of man" (verse 17), an ordinary term for a mortal, as God addresses Ezekiel. The chapter closes with Daniel ill and confounded, a reminder that revelation can overwhelm the one who receives it.

outline.t: The vision at Susa by the Ulai
The goat with a great horn
The little horn attacks the host and the sanctuary
The interpretation: Media, Persia, Greece, and a fierce king

doctrines.note: Empires rise and fall on schedule in this vision: the ram, the goat, the four horns. Even the arrogant king's power "will not be his own" (verse 24), and his end comes "not by human hands" (verse 25), that is, by God.

The attack on the daily sacrifice and the sanctuary is the climax of the little horn's evil. The chapter treats the desecration of worship as an assault on God himself, and it promises that the sanctuary will be set right.
God's people will be destroyed along with the mighty (verse 24). The vision does not hide the cost of faithfulness, but it limits the time of desolation and promises the oppressor's fall.

words.note: Tamid, continually, used here as a noun for the regular or daily sacrifice offered morning and evening. Its removal by the little horn (verse 11) is the central offense of the vision, and the same term returns in 11:31 and 12:11.

Tsadaq, to be right or to be put right. In verse 14 the sanctuary will be properly restored, literally made right or vindicated. It is the root of the words for righteousness and justice: restoring true worship is an act of God's justice.

Gabriel, the first angel named in the Bible. He appears again in 9:21 to explain the seventy weeks, and in Luke's Gospel he announces the births of John the Baptist and Jesus. In both testaments he brings understanding of God's timetable.

Qeren, horn, a standard Old Testament symbol of strength and royal power. The chapter tracks horns throughout: two on the ram, one on the goat, then four, then a little horn that grows great. Power is pictured as something that grows, breaks, and is replaced.

christ: The chapter looks forward to the Maccabean crisis rather than directly to Christ, and most interpreters agree that its primary fulfillment came under Antiochus IV. Yet it shaped how the New Testament speaks of the end. Jesus warned of "the abomination of desolation" described by Daniel (Matthew 24:15), and Paul describes a man of lawlessness who will exalt himself and seat himself in God's temple (2 Thessalonians 2:4), drawing on the pattern of the self-magnifying king in this chapter and in chapter 11. The promise that the oppressor will be broken "not by human hands" echoes the stone of 2:34, cut out without human hands, which the church reads as the kingdom that comes in Christ. The same Gabriel who explains this vision later announces to Mary that her son will reign over the house of Jacob forever (Luke 1:26-33).

hard.q: What do the 2,300 evenings and mornings mean?
hard.a: The phrase can be read two ways. Many take it as 2,300 evening and morning sacrifices, that is, 1,150 days, a little over three years; others take it as 2,300 full days, about six years and four months. Those who connect the vision with Antiochus IV note that the altar was desecrated in December 167 BC and rededicated in December 164 BC, three years later, and they see the 1,150 days as a close approximation of that period, perhaps counted from an earlier event such as the start of the persecution. Those who take 2,300 days look for a starting point in the troubles several years before the desecration. In the nineteenth century some historicist interpreters, who read prophetic days as years, used this verse to calculate Christ's return, most famously William Miller, whose prediction for 1844 was not fulfilled. Most interpreters today, conservative and critical alike, read the number as marking a limited, God-appointed period for the desolation of the sanctuary, whatever its exact reckoning.

questions: The ram and the goat each "became great" until something greater came along. What does this vision say about the permanence of any power you admire or fear?
The little horn attacked worship itself. Why might those who oppose God aim first at the practices of worship and prayer?
Daniel was exhausted and did not understand the vision, yet he got up and went about the king's business. How do you keep faithful in ordinary work when God's purposes are beyond your understanding?
